newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's growls over weak yen lack bite--dealers.
newsitem.headline: Japan's growls over weak yen lack bite--dealers.

text.p: They may growl, but Japanese authorities' comments deploring the yen's weakness lack any bite because Tokyo is too isolated within the Group of Seven to back its words with action, currency dealers say.

"The (Japanese) authorities may be willing to intervene in the market but won't be able to do so because such action wouldn't win endorsement from Japan's partners," said Shinichiro Maruyama, head of spot trading at the Industrial Bank of Japan.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told a parliamentary committee on Thursday that Japan will deal appropriately with an excessively strong or weak yen, Jiji news agency reported.

Asked about the dollar's rise against the yen to the mid-117 yen level overnight, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka also said on Thursday: "It's not desirable for the foreign exchange rate to fluctuate (wildly)."
Toshihiko Masaki, forex manager at Citibank N.A. Tokyo branch said: "The government is likely to show its discontent over the dollar's rally above 117 yen, at least in words.
"But it's unclear whether these words would be immediately backed up by action," added Masaki, referring to currency market intervention.
The dollar climbed to a fresh 46-month high of 117.48 yen in New York on Wednesday before it succumbed to selling for profits. It hit 117.03 yen in late Tokyo dealings on Thursday.

Operators in Tokyo believe Japan will be unable to openly sell dollars for yen by itself in light of a solid agreement for a strong dollar among the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations since April 1995.

Japan, which once loudly called on other nations to reverse a strong yen trend, has now started to speak out against a further decline of the yen, while other nations still openly favour a strong dollar.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated recently the Clinton administration's oft-stated support for a strong dollar. A strong dollar is seen bringing U.S. inflation down and contributing to stabilising U.S. financial markets.

German central bank President Hans Tietmeyer also said this week that the top industrial nations, called the Group of 10, have no cause for concern about exchange rate levels within Europe or between Europe and the United States.
Their stance reflects a strong desire to boost their exports and balance their budgets in a bid to meet tough criteria for membership in the European Union's single currency, to be launched in 1999.
Japan has its own problem to deal with -- the double headache of a weak yen and falling stocks.
"What the Japanese authorities are worrying about most is that the yen's fall will accompany further dives in the stock market," IBJ's Maruyama added.

Analysts said further falls in the Tokyo stock market would squeeze profits of financial institutions or even cause some institutions with serious bad loan problems to go bankrupt ahead of their fiscal book closings at the end of March.

"A further slide in the yen may also trigger a sell-off of Japanese stocks by foreign investors if the Nikkei 225 index falls below a long-term support of the key 150 on a dollar basis," said a currency manager at a leading Japanese bank.
The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed at 18,144.34 on a yen basis or about $155 in dollar terms.
Meanwhile, there was a whiff of rumour overnight that Japan may have sold dollars for yen at around 117.50 yen, but many dealers in Tokyo dismissed such a possibility.
"If Japan really bought the yen against the dollar visibly, the dollar would have surely fallen below 110.00 yen," said IBJ's Maruyama.
"The only feasible intervention for Japan may be yen buying against the German mark, which would indirectly slow the pace of the yen's decline against the dollar," said Maruyama.
European nations such as Germany might not oppose such a move as falls in the value of their currencies against the yen would make their exports to Japan more competitive, he said.
